records.title: Databricks / cloud deployment: DatabricksBackend, PySpark codegen, cloud recon, Workflow YAML export
records.body:
## Summary

`CLOUD=true` is referenced throughout the codebase but `DatabricksBackend` is not implemented and all generated code is always pandas/PostgreSQL. This issue defines the full cloud deployment path: PySpark codegen, `DatabricksBackend`, cloud-aware reconciliation, and a Databricks Workflow YAML in the post-acceptance export package.

## Scope

### A. Generated code format (CLOUD=true)

Primary output is **Python modules** (`.py` files), not notebooks. Each generated file opens with a `SparkSession` init. A generated `databricks_workflow.yml` wires the files as job tasks with dependencies mirroring the data lineage graph.

Notebooks are a UI concern — the Python modules can be imported into a Databricks notebook by the engineer if needed; we do not generate notebook format.

### B. PySpark translation rules

When `CLOUD=true`, LLM agent prompts use a different rule set:
- No `pandas` imports — all DataFrames are Spark DataFrames
- No `psycopg2` or local DB writes — outputs go to Delta tables or configurable storage paths
- `spark.read.csv(...)` / `spark.read.parquet(...)` replaces `pd.read_csv(...)`
- Aggregations use PySpark `.groupBy().agg()` not pandas `.groupby()`
- Output paths follow the target data lake convention (configurable via `DATABRICKS_DATA_ROOT`)

`CLOUD` flag must be resolved at **prompt time** — agents produce different code, not a post-processing pandas→PySpark transform.

### C. Data layer configuration

Three env vars control the target data layer:

| Var | Purpose | Default |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABRICKS_DATA_ROOT` | Storage path prefix (`abfss://...`, `s3://...`, `dbfs:/...`) | `dbfs:/rosetta` |
| `DATABRICKS_OUTPUT_FORMAT` | `delta` or `parquet` | `delta` |
| `DATABRICKS_CATALOG` | Unity Catalog name (empty = legacy Hive metastore) | `""` |

### D. DatabricksBackend implementation

`src/worker/compute/databricks.py` implements the `ComputeBackend` interface:

- `execute(code, job_id)` — submits code via Databricks Jobs API 2.1 `runs/submit`; returns a run handle
- `get_result(run_id)` — polls until complete; fetches stdout/stderr output
- Auth: `DATABRICKS_HOST` + `DATABRICKS_TOKEN` env vars; use `databricks-sdk` Python package (not direct REST calls)

### E. Cloud-aware reconciliation

`recon.py` currently assumes local file paths. When `CLOUD=true`:
- Reference data is read from the configured `DATABRICKS_DATA_ROOT` path (not from `/uploads/`)
- A cloud-aware file reader abstraction wraps both local and remote reads
- Recon results structure is unchanged — only the data source changes

### F. Databricks Workflow YAML export

Added to the post-acceptance export package (see issue #68):
- One task per generated Python file
- Task dependencies derived from the job's lineage graph
- Cluster config stubbed with sensible defaults (overridable via env)
- Engineer runs `databricks bundle deploy` to deploy the pipeline

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] `DatabricksBackend` class in `src/worker/compute/databricks.py` implementing `ComputeBackend`
- [ ] `CLOUD=true` routes to `DatabricksBackend`; `CLOUD=false` routes to `LocalBackend` (no change)
- [ ] LLM agent prompts branch on `CLOUD` flag at call time — PySpark rules when true, pandas rules when false
- [ ] Generated PySpark code uses `SparkSession`, `spark.read.*`, `.groupBy().agg()`, Delta/Parquet writes
- [ ] `DATABRICKS_DATA_ROOT`, `DATABRICKS_OUTPUT_FORMAT`, `DATABRICKS_CATALOG` env vars documented in `.env.example`
- [ ] Cloud recon reads reference data from `DATABRICKS_DATA_ROOT` when `CLOUD=true`
- [ ] Post-acceptance zip includes `databricks_workflow.yml` when `CLOUD=true`
- [ ] `make test` exits 0 (DatabricksBackend unit-tested with mocked SDK calls)

## Out of scope

- Terraform / Helm for infrastructure provisioning
- Service principal auth (PAT is sufficient for now; SP deferred to F14)
- Databricks Asset Bundles full config (workflow YAML is a stub — engineer completes cluster/permissions config)
- Unity Catalog table ACLs

## Dependencies

- Post-acceptance export package (#68) — Workflow YAML is bundled there
- F14 (auth) — service principal auth replaces PAT
- `databricks-sdk` added to `pyproject.toml`

records.title: hasXBridge/hasZBridge termination rests on undocumented parity guards
records.body:
`BuildingInfo.hasXBridge` (`:1349-1359`, delegate `computeXBridge` `:1361-1407`) and `hasZBridge`
(`:1411-1418`, `computeZBridge` `:1420-1479`) recurse into their neighbours. Termination now rests
on parity guards that are not documented as termination conditions:

- `BuildingInfo.java:1368,1374,1388` — `if (coord.chunkZ() % 2 != 0 && (getZmin().hasXBridge(...) != null || getZmax().hasXBridge(...) != null)) return null;`
- `BuildingInfo.java:1432,1442,1460` — the `chunkX % 2` mirror for Z bridges
- `BuildingInfo.java:1428,1439,1457` — `if (hasXBridge(provider) != null) return null;`

plus the memoisation flags at `:102-103` (`xBridgeTypeCalculated` / `zBridgeTypeCalculated`), written
at `:1356-1357`, `:1416-1417` and bulk-written into neighbours at `:1401-1403`, `:1473-1475`.

The comment at `:1348` explains the parity as a *priority* rule ("bridges at even chunk Z get higher
priority"), not as the thing that stops the recursion — and the deliberate no-lock note at `:83-93`
compounds it. If someone changes the parity rule for layout reasons they can turn this into a
stack overflow or an infinite walk without any local sign that they have.

Wanted: document the termination argument at the guards, or make it explicit (depth bound /
explicit visited set) rather than emergent.

---
**Reference corrections (2026-08-10 audit — code moved ~38 lines up; defect and quoted guard text unchanged):** `hasXBridge` `:1349-1359` → `:1311-1321`; `computeXBridge` `:1361-1407` → `:1323-1378`; `hasZBridge` `:1411-1418` → `:1381-1389`; `computeZBridge` `:1420-1479` → `:1391-1455`; X parity guards `:1368,1374,1388` → `:1338,1344,1358`; Z parity guards `:1432,1442,1460` → `:1407,1417,1435`; `hasXBridge != null` guards `:1428,1439,1457` → `:1403,1414,1432`; memo flags `:102-103` unchanged; flag writes `:1356-1357`/`:1416-1417` → `:1318-1319`/`:1386-1387`; bulk neighbour writes `:1401-1403`/`:1473-1475` → `:1371-1373`/`:1448-1450`; no-lock note `:83-93` → `:84-91`; priority comment `:1348` → `:1310`.

New since filing: #100 added a planned-bridge early return (`computeXBridge :1324-1331`, `computeZBridge :1392-1400`) that exits before the parity walk when `PrimaryBridgePlanner` owns the chunk — narrows the reachable cases, changes nothing about the termination argument.

records.title: Audit findings — security, concurrency, reliability, scalability
records.body:
Audit of the implementation against the fourteen failure modes the design set out to prevent. Each finding was checked against the code, not against the design doc's claims about the code. **Thirteen of the fourteen hold**; the sub-issues below are what does not, plus the latent items worth an explicit decision before they become real.

Verified on branch `main` at `539c3d7`. `npm run typecheck` passes.

Source: `.scratch/access-control/issues/audit-findings.md`

### Findings (severity order)

| # | Finding | Severity | Status |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| F1 | A retried refresh revokes the user's entire session family | high | ready-for-agent |
| F2 | Nothing stops a read replica from restoring revoked access | medium (latent) | needs-triage |
| F3 | The version-skew CI gate is a no-op unless the deploy pipeline sets one variable | medium | needs-info |
| F4 | Login against an unknown tenant slug is neither throttled nor audited | low | ready-for-agent |
| F5 | The shard-key cache is never invalidated | informational | wontfix |

### What was checked and found sound

Listed so a later reader knows these were verified against code rather than assumed, and does not re-audit them.

| Failure mode | Where it is handled |
| --- | --- |
| Connection pooling leaks | `tenant-database.ts:105` — `BEGIN` + `set_config(..., true)` per transaction, never a session-level `SET`. Every background job that takes a raw pool does the same with its own sweep setting. RLS is `ENABLE` **and** `FORCE` on every tenant-owned table; `app` is explicitly `NOBYPASSRLS` (`002_app_role.sql:21`). |
| Confused deputy | `payroll.controller.ts` — `InternalTokenGuard` then `AuthzGuard`. The second re-evaluates the acting user's own snapshot and knows nothing about the caller (§8.3 rule 5). |
| Stolen token reuse | Opaque refresh tokens, stored as `sha256` only, rotated in one transaction, with family-wide revocation on replay. |
| Insider / support access | `013_support_grants.sql` — ≤4 hours, one tenant, reason and ticket required, `approved_by <> requested_by` enforced by the database. No bypass role exists. |
| Token bloat and staleness | `token-signer.ts:57` — `iss/sub/tid/sid/typ/aud/iat/exp/jti` and nothing else (D4). Even the support token omits the access level. |
| Concurrent admin edits | `roles.repository.ts:198` — compare-and-set on `version`; the controller makes the version mandatory, so there is no implicit-overwrite path. |
| Dropped invalidation events | `snapshot-cache.ts:77` — both cached tiers re-check version and epoch. Pub/sub is the optimisation; the counters are the guarantee (N4 runs with pub/sub off). |
| Temporal expiry | Two sweepers schedule a rebuild a second after each stated expiry; correctness does not depend on them, only timeliness. |
| Cache stampede | Single-flight `inflight` map plus ±20% jitter on every TTL. |
| Redis / auth outage | Circuit breaker, longer degraded TTL, stale serving up to a ceiling, then **503** rather than 403. |
| Org tree load | Materialized path with a `text_pattern_ops` prefix index; no recursive CTE on the hot path. |

records.title: Slow Docker builds in `nox -s run` due to layer cache invalidation
records.body:
# Docker Build Optimization: Dependency Layer Caching for `nox -s run`

## Summary
`nox -s run` was rebuilding the expensive Docker dependency layer whenever application code changed. The root cause was Docker layer ordering rather than Nox itself: the Dockerfile copied `app/` before running `uv sync`, so changing a Python file invalidated the layer containing Streamlit and its dependencies. The Dockerfile and Nox session have now been optimized.

## Previous Behavior
The session ran `docker build` (pulling or verifying base images, copying dependencies and application code, installing Streamlit and all dependencies, building the final image) followed by `docker run` (starting Streamlit). `docker build` ran unconditionally, and application changes caused the complete dependency installation to run again.

## Root Cause
The Dockerfile previously copied the application code before installing dependencies: it copied pyproject.toml, uv.lock, README.md, and LICENSE, then copied the app folder, and only afterward ran `uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-editable`. Docker builds images layer by layer and can only reuse a layer if that layer and every preceding layer remain unchanged. Because the app copy appeared before the sync step, changing a file such as app/main.py invalidated both the application source layer and the dependency installation layer. This caused Streamlit and its complete dependency tree to be processed again even when pyproject.toml and uv.lock had not changed.

## Why This Was Costly
Streamlit has a relatively large dependency tree, including Streamlit, Pandas, NumPy, PyArrow, Pillow, Altair, PyDeck, GitPython, and related web-server components. The Dockerfile also enables bytecode compilation via UV_COMPILE_BYTECODE=1, which can improve container startup time but adds work during image construction. PyArrow was the most expensive dependency during the initial cold build.

## Adopted Docker Solution
Third-party dependencies are now installed before the application source is copied. First, pyproject.toml and uv.lock are copied and `uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-install-project` runs with a BuildKit cache mount targeting /root/.cache/uv. Then README.md, LICENSE, and the app folder are copied, followed by `uv sync --frozen --no-dev --no-editable`, again using the cache mount. This creates two distinct installation layers: a large third-party dependency layer and a small local application package layer. The cache mount allows downloaded packages to be reused if the dependency layer must be rebuilt.

## Resulting Behavior
Editing app/main.py invalidates only the COPY app layer. The Streamlit dependency layer remains cached, so only the local application package is rebuilt before the final image is assembled and started. The expensive dependency layer is rebuilt only when pyproject.toml or uv.lock change. Changes to application code or documentation no longer reinstall the complete Streamlit dependency tree.

## Default Incremental Build
The default command remains `uv run nox -s run`, which performs an incremental Docker build before starting the container. This stays the recommended default because it guarantees the running container contains the latest application code. With the optimized layer ordering, application-only changes now produce a much faster build.

## Skipping the Build
The adopted solution uses a Nox session argument instead of an environment variable: `uv run nox -s run -- --no-build`. The first `--` separates Nox options from arguments passed to the run session. When `--no-build` is provided, the session skips `docker build`, verifies that the requested image exists locally, fails immediately if the image is missing, and starts the existing image. The session also rejects unsupported arguments.

## Trade-off
Using `--no-build` starts the application faster, but any source-code changes made since the previous image build will not be included. Use `uv run nox -s run` after changing application code, dependencies, the Dockerfile, or image configuration. Use `uv run nox -s run -- --no-build` when restarting an image that is already up to date.

## Additional Configuration
The host port can still be changed with APP_PORT, e.g. `APP_PORT=8080 uv run nox -s run`, and it can be combined with --no-build as `APP_PORT=8080 uv run nox -s run -- --no-build`. The Docker image name and tag remain configurable through DOCKER_IMAGE and DOCKER_TAG.

## Validation
The optimized Dockerfile was validated successfully with Docker BuildKit. The first cold build downloaded and installed the complete dependency tree, while the local application package installation took only a few seconds. The following build reported all Docker layers as CACHED. Dockerfile validation completed without warnings, and the Nox configuration passes Ruff and formatting checks.

## Outcome
The adopted solution provides two execution modes. `uv run nox -s run` incrementally builds and starts the image, recommended for the default

records.body:
**📨 Subject**: Confusing numbers in actual time in explain analyze output of
 recursive query when jit is used

**📅 Date:** 2024-05-24 14:19:55
**📤 Sender:** "Machytka, Josef" <Josef(dot)Machytka(at)netapp(dot)com>
**📥 Receiver:** "pgsql-bugs(at)lists(dot)postgresql(dot)org" <pgsql-bugs(at)lists(dot)postgresql(dot)org>
**📮 Message ID:** `BN8PR06MB5380E8A973D482231284A466F0F52@BN8PR06MB5380.namprd06.prod.outlook.com`

**📝 Message :**
Hello nice people.

I would like to report one problem with EXPLAIN ANALYZE output from recursive query when JIT is ON and OS supports jit, so JIT was used. It is most likely not new , but it was very confusing for the client and online research did not help them. Therefore, I want to send this email also as a reference for the future.

Client had recursive query using quite complicated underlying views, resulting in scans over multiple tables. They optimized the most problematic steps with new indexes but then the explain analyze output suddenly showed a long run on previously quick step. And there was seemingly nothing else to optimize on this step.

Since total time of the recursive loop in the output roughly corresponded to the total JIT time, we asked the client to run query with JIT = OFF. And problem was gone and query much quicker.  
Problem was that JIT time was added always to the slowest step in the recursive loop, which caused very paradoxical behavior - previously quick step suddenly seemingly slowed down without any clear reason.

Details:

* Client has recursive query which uses quite complicated underlying views resulting in processing of multiple tables:

with recursive traversal as  
(select "Type", "Id", 0 as level, '' as rel_type from myview1 where "Id" = 'xxxxxx'  
union  
select t2."Type", t2."Id", level+1, e."Type"  
from  
traversal t1  
join  
myview2 e on t1."Id" = e."FromId" and e."Type" = 'xxx'  
join  
myview1 t2 on e."ToId" = t2."Id"  
)  
select * from traversal;

* They did several optimization but Recursive Union part stayed slow in all cases with roughly similar run time:  
-> Recursive Union (cost=0.28..1313656908.74 rows=104384767268 width=84) (actual time=228.732..228.833 rows=2 loops=1)  
-> Recursive Union (cost=0.28..1313352949.93 rows=104360450528 width=84) (actual time=240.739..240.877 rows=2 loops=1)

* Very confusing was that previously quick step in the first run was suddenly very slow in the second run without any change at all in this step.  
* first run: -> Index Only Scan using "mytable_pkey" on myschema."mytable" t_7 (cost=0.43..1.55 rows=1 width=48) (actual time=0.014..0.015 rows=1 loops=1)  
* second run: -> Index Only Scan using "mytable_pkey" on myschema."mytable" t_7 (cost=0.43..1.55 rows=1 width=48) (actual time=240.650..240.652 rows=1 loops=1)"

* Difference was that optimized step was now quicker that this one and the JIT time was roughly added in the explain analyze output to this now slowest step of recursive loop.

JIT:  
Functions: 48  
Options: Inlining true, Optimization true, Expressions true, Deforming true  
Timing: Generation 3.489 ms, Inlining 16.984 ms, Optimization 115.833 ms, Emission 107.853 ms, Total 244.158 ms

* Without JIT query ends in just few milliseconds.

Best regards

records.title: Backlog triage: a tiered order for the remaining 310 open issues
records.body:
# Triage order for the open backlog

311 issues are open. This orders the **310** that aren't this one into a single tiered read:
what to tackle first, and why. It is a working document — order is a recommendation, not a
contract, and anything can be pulled forward when it blocks real use.

The ordering principle, in priority order:

1. **Don't lose data.** A bug that destroys or silently corrupts an inventory outranks
   everything, because the user cannot undo it.
2. **Don't be wrong.** Data that is present but incorrect (money, dates, sync
   convergence) is worse than data that is visibly missing.
3. **Fix what's unusable.** Features that are broken, unreachable, or truncated in
   normal use.
4. **Then make it fast, accessible, translated, documented, and richer.**

Schema-shaped fixes are deliberately front-loaded: the project is pre-1.0 with a single
squashed migration baseline, so changing a column type is cheap **now** and expensive
after release.

Within each tier the order is severity, most urgent first: silent corruption outranks a
loud failure, a defect reachable in normal use outranks one needing an unusual setup, and
a cheap fix with a wide blast radius outranks an expensive one with a narrow radius. Where
two issues share a root cause or one fix closes both, they sit adjacent and say so.

---

## Tier 1 — Data loss, boot integrity and the recovery path

The user cannot undo any of these. Several are worse than plain loss: they *report success*
over a failure, so the user finds out later, with no copy to go back to.

> Do 1–5 first. Four of the five destroy or discard data while telling the user the
> operation succeeded.

1. #502 — Three destructive paths delete data straight after a download that cannot report whether it saved
2. #638 — A sync that merges then fails to push discards its conflict records, and the overwritten edit cannot be recovered afterwards
3. #654 — Escape, the backdrop and the ✕ ignore a dialog's in-flight guard, so a dismissed restore still wipes the database and the failure lands on an unmounted handler
4. #647 — Finalising a project consumes the whole matched item, ignoring the BOM line's quantity: an item with 500 on hand is archived entire
5. #639 — A failure while re-hydrating images after a restore is reported as "the restore failed", though the database has already been replaced (same post-overwrite reporting hazard as 3)
6. #504 — A real out-of-space failure never raises the storage tier, so Triage and the Hard Stop stay dormant while every write fails
7. #554 — A request's timeout runs while it is still queued, so the caller is told a write was undone that the worker then commits
8. #499 — A new build's service worker precaches into the live cache, so a refresh takes an update the user never accepted — and lands on the reset screen unwarned
9. #587 — "Pause & close" in the guided stock-take discards every count typed at the current location
10. #576 — Switching tabs in the item dialog silently discards unsaved Details edits
11. #588 — Deleting a purchase order or one of its lines is a single unconfirmed click, next to "Cancel order"
12. #677 — The serialised "How many" count has no upper bound: 10,000 commits ten thousand records in one transaction with no undo, and an overflowed value loops until the tab dies
13. #675 — Editing a purchase price to an unparseable value silently erases it, and reports a successful save
14. #205 — Nothing ever backs up automatically, and every backup nag can be silenced permanently (the mitigation for everything above — worth doing early even though it is an enhancement)

## Tier 2 — Sync convergence and merge invariants

Data that is present but wrong, or a device that stops converging and says nothing. Several
of these are permanent: the failing plan is recomputed identically forever.

> 15 and 16 are the two newest and the two worst: one silently halves real stock, the other
> bricks sync on a name a user is entitled to type.

15. #633 — Counting the same shelf on two devices halves it: an absolute cycle count is captured as a relative delta and both are applied
16. #679 — The collision resolver folds names more widely than the UNIQUE index does, so a merge can abort on the very constraint it exists to avoid (same natural-key family as 19 and 20)
17. #535 — `checkouts` is ordered before `projects` in `SYNC_TABLES`, so any database holding a project loan cannot be cloned or replace-restored
18. #602 — A merge or restore aborts with a raw foreign-key error when a self-referencing row is applied before its parent
19. #603 — The same supplier created on two devices permanently blocks sync: `suppliers.name_key` has no natural-key collision rule
20. #538 — Natural-key collision resolution is missing from backup restore and the tombstone-TTL clone (the same machinery as 16 and 19 — one pass covers all three)
21. #604 — The stock-delta capture triggers have no DELETE arm

records.title: [Maintenance] CI/CD: Canonical license audit on transitive dependencies (fleet-wide)
records.body:
## Scope

Add a canonical license-audit check that runs on every PR and on a weekly schedule, fanned out via the standard template-sync flow so every downstream Wolfgang.* library inherits the same posture without per-repo plumbing.

## What we're solving

Risk: a transitive dependency silently introduces a license that's incompatible with the MIT license downstream Wolfgang.* libraries ship under.

Concrete scenarios this catches:

1. **GPL/AGPL contamination via transitive bumps.** A direct dependency bumps and adds a transitive on something GPL-licensed. Redistributors of the MIT-licensed library then have a compliance problem — and they have no way to know it happened, because the GPL package is several levels deep.
2. **License changes in direct deps.** A package switches from MIT to BSL or Elastic License 2.0 between versions (this has happened with Redis, MongoDB, Elasticsearch, Sentry). The version bump still type-checks and tests pass.
3. **"Unknown" license** — package author shipped without a license expression at all. Some procurement policies treat that as worse than a permissive incompatible license.
4. **Audit trail for compliance.** Larger NuGet consumers (regulated industries, F500) periodically scan their transitive graph against an internal allowlist. Having our own audit run on every PR means we can point to a tested-baseline when their security team asks.

## Proposed canonical implementation (3 files)

### 1. `scripts/Audit-Licenses.ps1`

- Walks every src csproj
- Invokes `dotnet list package --include-transitive --format json`
- For each (package, version), resolves the SPDX license expression from `~/.nuget/packages/<id>/<v>/<id>.nuspec` (`<license type="expression">…</license>`)
- Joins against the allowlist in `license-policy.json`
- Treats packages with no license expression as `unknown` (fails unless explicitly listed under `policy.allowed_unknown`)
- Reports findings as a markdown table; fails with `throw` (exits non-zero from the workflow's `pwsh` host)

### 2. `license-policy.json` (root)

```jsonc
{
  "allowed_licenses": [
    "MIT", "Apache-2.0", "BSD-3-Clause", "BSD-2-Clause",
    "MS-PL", "MS-RL", "0BSD", "Unlicense", "CC0-1.0"
  ],
  "allowed_packages": [
    // Explicit per-package exceptions where the SPDX expression is wrong
    // upstream or where the license is acceptable case-by-case (e.g. MS
    // reference assemblies).
  ],
  "allowed_unknown": [
    // Packages with no <license> in the nuspec that we've manually verified.
  ]
}
```

### 3. `.github/workflows/license-audit.yaml`

- Triggers: `pull_request` (so Dependabot bumps run against it), `schedule` (weekly, catches mid-week license changes upstream), `workflow_dispatch`
- Standard hardening: `permissions: contents: read`, `actions/checkout` with `persist-credentials: false`
- One step that calls `pwsh ./scripts/Audit-Licenses.ps1` after `dotnet restore`
- No `gh-pages` / `releases` write — pure validation

## File-scope classification

- `scripts/Audit-Licenses.ps1` — **unprotected**
- `license-policy.json` (root) — **unprotected**
- `.github/workflows/license-audit.yaml` — **protected**

So the canonical fanout PR is **mixed**, targets `vNext` per the standard branching model, and rides the protected-files merge train with the next vNext promotion.

## Out of scope

- **FOSSA / dotnet-licenses commercial tooling.** The proposed implementation is self-contained (PowerShell + the SPDX expressions already in NuGet nuspecs). If we need a richer policy engine (sub-license analysis, attribution-file generation), FOSSA's free-tier OSS account is a follow-up — not the canonical default.
- **Examples / benchmarks / tests projects.** Only `src/` is audited; benchmarks and tests can pull in anything (they don't ship).
- **License-file generation for the .nupkg.** Already handled by `<PackageLicenseExpression>` in the canonical csproj metadata.

## Fan-out plan

1. Land this PR on repo-template `main`
2. Run `template-drift-scan` to confirm downstream repos surface the three new files as drift
3. Use `bulk-repo-pr` to open per-repo canonical PRs adding the three files
4. Each downstream PR will need admin-bypass for the workflow file (mixed PR, but the workflow path is protected)

## Per-repo issues already filed

The same gap is tracked per-repo on every active fleet repo as `CI/CD: License audit on transitive dependencies`. Those issues will close on this canonical PR's fanout.

## Notes

- Tier-1 foundation task — part of the canonical CI/CD set.
- The per-repo cost when the audit fires is ~0 today for most libraries (1–3 direct deps, ~5–15 transitives, all MIT/Apache-2.0). The value is asymmetric — it's cheap insurance that catches a rare, expensive class of incidents.
- Board: https://github.com/users/Chris-Wolfgang/projects/6

records.title: Dossiers have no outgoing-dependency section — only "External consumers" exists; half the graph is invisible to readers
records.body:
## Symptom

Every dossier in the corpus (747 of them) has exactly six sections: Purpose, Invariants, Gotchas, Cross-cutting concerns, External consumers, Open questions. The only edge-derived section is `## External consumers` — the **inbound** edges (reverse dependencies).

There is no section for the node's own **outbound** edges (what this node depends on). A reader looking at a function dossier learns who calls it but not what it calls. A reader of a class dossier learns its consumers but not its base class, its imports, or what it instantiates.

```
$ grep -h '^## ' classes/*.md functions/*.md | sort | uniq -c
    747 ## Purpose
    747 ## Open questions
    747 ## Invariants
    747 ## Gotchas
    747 ## External consumers
    747 ## Cross-cutting concerns
```

## Root cause

The asymmetry is wired all the way through:

1. **Draft prompt** (`lib/cli/dossier.py:183-190`) loads `deps_idx` (the reverse-dependents index) and formats the top 15 as a "Direct dependents" block. There is no corresponding load of the node's own `edges_out`.
2. **Dossier template** in the same file requires `## External consumers` as a section; no `## Dependencies` slot.
3. **All 747 existing dossiers** were written from the asymmetric prompt against the asymmetric template, so retro-fixing the prompt doesn't fix the corpus.

The model writing the dossier has to scrape outgoing dependencies out of the raw source excerpt, with no graph-supplied data. This is the same fabrication failure mode as #48: when the prompt doesn't carry a structured input, the LLM invents one.

## Fix path

Three paired changes:

### 1. Add an outgoing block to the draft prompt

In `cmd_dossier_draft`, after the dependents block:

- Read the node's own `edges_out`.
- Filter out `defines` edges (they're intrinsic to the node, not dependencies — Boat's columns aren't dependencies of Boat).
- Group by `kind`: `extends`, `imports`, `calls`, `instantiates`, `references`.
- Format like the dependents block: top 15 with file:line and confidence, "+N more" tail.

~20 lines.

### 2. Add a required `## Dependencies` section to the dossier template

Slot between `## Invariants` and `## Cross-cutting concerns`. Prompt instruction: "Group by relationship kind (inherits/imports/calls/instantiates/references). Be concrete; name files and symbols. Note where dependencies are external libraries vs in-corpus."

### 3. Backfill the existing 747 dossiers

Two paths:

- **Re-draft each** through the existing LLM pipeline. Expensive (tokens × 747) and inherits whatever fabrication risks exist in the current prompt (see #48).
- **Structural-only injection** — a deterministic pass that reads each node's `edges_out`, renders a `## Dependencies` section purely from data, and marks the dossier `status: structural_only` (new status). The prose sections remain whatever was previously authored; only the structural section is machine-rendered.

Recommend the structural-only path first. It's deterministic, cheap, and creates the slot. Subsequent `dossier-rank` cycles can re-promote dossiers from `structural_only` → `llm_drafted` → `current` as humans review them.

Bonus: structural-only rendering also handles the dossier-redraft problem when reverse-deps shift (related to the stale-detection issue, forthcoming) — the structural sections always reflect current data without re-asking an LLM.

## Interaction with other gaps

- **#55 coverage caveats**: outgoing-section completeness depends on what extractors capture. Where the graph is known-blind (ORM, FK, etc.), the outgoing section should defer to the coverage-caveats section rather than claim completeness.
- **Confidence taxonomy (#53)**: outgoing edges currently include both "exact" and "unresolved" — the section should group these and label the unresolved bucket honestly (e.g. "Dependencies (with N unresolved targets — see Coverage caveats)").

## Test surface

- Existing dossier-draft tests should be extended to verify the outgoing block appears in the prompt and is populated with the node's filtered edges_out.
- Structural-only injection: golden tests for a known node (e.g. a known-stable class in the test fixtures), verify the rendered `## Dependencies` section matches expected text.

## Related

- #48 dossier-draft fabricates — same root cause (prompt doesn't supply structured inputs)
- #55 coverage caveats — pairs with this; together they make the dossier honest in both directions
- Dossier-draft two-pass issue (forthcoming) — the structural-only rendering is essentially the "structural pass" of a two-pass design

records.title: Grant where clause cannot express recursive folder tree walk for permission inheritance
records.body:
## Context

While implementing hierarchical folder permissions for cfast-wiki (DanielMSchmidt/cfast#292), I discovered that the `@cfast/permissions` grant `where` clause cannot express a recursive tree walk in a single SQL expression.

## What was needed

Per-folder visibility inheritance: folders have `visibility` (inherit/workspace/restricted) and `allowedRoles`. To determine if a user can read a document, we need to walk up the folder tree from the document's folder until we find a non-"inherit" visibility, then check if the user's role is in `allowedRoles`.

## What was tried

Expressing this in a grant `where` clause:

```ts
grant("read", "documents", {
  where: (doc, user, lookups) => {
    // Need: walk doc.folderId -> parent -> parent... until visibility != "inherit"
    // Problem: this callback must return a Drizzle SQL expression for a single query
    // A recursive CTE or multi-query walk is not expressible here
  }
})
```

The `with` option for prerequisite lookups is also insufficient because:
1. It runs once per request, not once per row
2. It doesn't have access to the current row's `folderId` to walk that specific tree path
3. Even if it did, the result needs to be a SQL `WHERE` fragment, not a JS boolean

## What failed

There is no way to express "walk the folder tree for each document row and check visibility" as a single Drizzle SQL `WHERE` clause. SQLite supports recursive CTEs (`WITH RECURSIVE`), but the grant `where` callback only produces a Drizzle `SQL` expression that gets AND'd into the main query -- it cannot restructure the query to use a CTE.

## Workaround used

Server-side tree walk in the route loader using `db.unsafe()`:

1. Load all folders in the workspace in a single query
2. Walk the tree in memory to compute effective visibility per folder (with caching)
3. Filter documents after the DB query based on the computed visibility
4. Return filtered results

This works but has limitations:
- Permission filtering happens in application code, not in the DB layer
- `_can.read` on documents doesn't automatically reflect folder visibility
- The pattern requires manual enforcement in every route that loads documents

## Suggested enhancement

Consider supporting one or more of:
1. **CTE-based where clauses** -- allow grant `where` to return a query fragment that uses `WITH RECURSIVE`
2. **Row-level where with access to related rows** -- a `where` that can join/subquery related tables
3. **Computed permission columns** -- a way to define a permission that derives from a related entity's permission
4. **Pre-filter hook** -- a callback that runs after the query but before `_can` annotation, allowing application-level filtering that integrates with the permission system

Ref: DanielMSchmidt/cfast#292

records.title: feat: Task Dependencies / DAG Execution Support
records.body:
## Overview

Enable task execution order relationships through dependencies, allowing tasks to run only after prerequisite tasks complete successfully. This transforms CodeGeass from a simple CRON scheduler into a powerful DAG (Directed Acyclic Graph) execution engine.

## Problem Statement

Users often have related tasks that should run in sequence:
- "Run tests" must complete before "Deploy to staging"
- "Code review" must pass before "Create PR"
- Multiple parallel tasks should complete before "Send Summary Report"

Currently, users must set CRON schedules with artificial time gaps, hoping previous tasks finish in time. There's no way to express "run task B only if task A succeeds."

**Pain points:**
- Race conditions when dependent tasks overlap
- Wasted execution when prerequisites fail
- No visibility into task relationships
- Manual coordination required for complex workflows

## Proposed Solution

### High-Level Design

Add dependency support to tasks, allowing users to define execution relationships. Tasks can depend on one or more other tasks, with configurable conditions (success, failure, complete).

### Architecture Changes

```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Task Entity Extensions                    │
│                                                              │
│  Task                                                        │
│  ├── depends_on: list[TaskDependency]                       │
│  │   └── TaskDependency: {task_id, condition}               │
│  └── trigger_mode: "schedule" | "dependency" | "both"       │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    DAG Resolver (NEW)                        │
│  src/codegeass/scheduling/dag_resolver.py                   │
│                                                              │
│  ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────┐     ┌──────────────────┐     │
│  │ Validate │────▶│ Topo Sort│────▶│ Get Ready Tasks  │     │
│  │ (cycles) │     │ (Kahn's) │     │ (deps satisfied) │     │
│  └──────────┘     └──────────┘     └──────────────────┘     │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
                              │
                              ▼
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    Scheduler Extensions                      │
│                                                              │
│  Scheduler                                                   │
│  ├── run_dag(root_task_id) -> list[ExecutionResult]         │
│  ├── run_with_dependencies(task) -> ExecutionResult         │
│  └── get_dependency_chain(task_id) -> list[Task]            │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```

### Design Patterns Used

- **Topological Sort (Kahn's Algorithm)**: Determine safe execution order without cycles
- **Strategy Pattern**: Different dependency conditions (success, failure, complete)
- **Observer Pattern**: Notify dependent tasks when prerequisites complete

### Code Changes Required

#### 1. New Files to Create

| File Path | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `src/codegeass/scheduling/dag_resolver.py` | DAG validation, topological sort, cycle detection |
| `src/codegeass/core/dependency.py` | TaskDependency value object |
| `dashboard/frontend/src/pages/DAG.tsx` | DAG visualization page |
| `dashboard/frontend/src/components/dag/DAGVisualization.tsx` | Interactive graph component |

#### 2. Files to Modify

| File Path | Changes |
|-----------|---------|
| `src/codegeass/core/entities.py` | Add `depends_on`, `trigger_mode` fields to Task |
| `src/codegeass/storage/task_repository.py` | Handle dependency serialization/deserialization |
| `src/codegeass/scheduling/scheduler.py` | Add `run_dag()`, `run_with_dependencies()` methods |
| `src/codegeass/cli/commands/task.py` | Add dependency CLI commands |
| `dashboard/backend/routers/tasks.py` | Add DAG endpoints |
| `dashboard/frontend/src/components/TaskForm.tsx` | Add dependency selector |

#### 3. API Changes

| Endpoint | Method | Description |
|----------|--------|-------------|
| `/api/tasks/{id}/dependencies` | GET | Get task dependencies |
| `/api/tasks/{id}/dependencies` | PUT | Update task dependencies |
| `/api/tasks/{id}/dependents` | GET | Get tasks that depend on this task |
| `/api/dag/validate` | POST | Validate DAG for cycles |
| `/api/dag/run/{root_task_id}` | POST | Execute DAG from root |

#### 4. Storage Changes

Update `config/schedules.yaml` schema:

```yaml
tasks:
  - id: abc123
    name: run-tests
    schedule: "0 9 * * 1-5"
    trigger_mode: schedule
    # Entry point - no dependencies

  - id: def456
    name: deploy-staging
    depends_on:
      - task_id: abc123
        condition: success
    trigger_mode: dependency  # Only runs when tests pass
    # No schedule needed
